fields.definition: The group of lower-pitched, typically wound strings on a stringed instrument (on a six-string guitar, the E, A and D strings) and the lower-frequency register they produce. It is contrasted with the treble-string region formed by the higher, thinner strings.
fields.plain_english: The thicker, lower-sounding strings on a guitar or similar instrument, and the deep tones they make. Think of the left-hand end of a piano, but for strings.
fields.purpose_function: It labels the low end of a stringed instrument so players and engineers can tune, discuss, and capture those notes separately, since the wound bass strings carry the harmonic foundation and behave differently from treble strings.
fields.practical_application: An engineer positions or angles a mic to balance the bass-string region against the treble strings, and may use EQ so the wound low strings do not sound boomy or dull in the recording.
common_mistakes: Assuming the bass-string region only needs low-frequency EQ, when its note fundamentals and playing noise span a wide range
Confusing the bass-string region of a guitar with a separate bass guitar
Miking only over the soundhole, which exaggerates the boom from the wound low strings
scenario_contexts: Balancing the low strings against the high strings when close-miking an acoustic guitar
Applying gentle EQ so the wound E and A strings do not dominate a fingerpicked part
Discussing which strings carry the low end during a tracking session

fields.definition: The set of an instrument's lower-pitched bass strings treated as a single group, such as the wound bass strings of a guitar or the long, thick strings on the bass side of a piano or harp. The term refers to the strings themselves rather than to a frequency range.
fields.plain_english: The bunch of thick, low-sounding strings on an instrument, grouped together. On a piano these are the long strings at the left end.
fields.purpose_function: Grouping the bass strings lets players, tuners, and engineers address the low strings as a unit for tuning, damping, or miking, because they share construction and tonal behavior.
fields.practical_application: When recording a grand piano or harp, an engineer places or aims a microphone to capture the bass-string section evenly with the rest of the instrument.
common_mistakes: Treating the bass-string section as a separate instrument rather than part of the whole
Placing a mic so close to the bass strings that the section overpowers the treble strings
Forgetting that wound bass strings lose brightness as they age and dull the section's tone
scenario_contexts: Positioning a piano mic to balance the bass-string section against the treble
Checking tuning across the bass-string section of a harp before a take
Explaining to a client why the low strings sound duller than the high strings

fields.definition: On an instrument with paired or grouped strings (a course), an unevenness between the strings of the same course in loudness, tuning, tone, or string age, so the pair no longer sounds as one unified note. It commonly appears on 12-string guitars, mandolins, and lutes.
fields.plain_english: On instruments where strings come in pairs, it is when the two strings of a pair do not match. One may be louder or slightly out of tune, so the pair sounds uneven.
fields.purpose_function: The term flags a specific fault so it can be diagnosed and corrected; a balanced course produces the rich, chorused sound that paired strings are meant to give.
fields.practical_application: A tech listens for beating or a weak string within each course and fixes it by tuning both strings precisely, matching string gauges, or replacing a dead string before tracking.
common_mistakes: Tuning only the main string of a course and ignoring its octave or unison partner
Blaming the room or mic for a beating, uneven sound that is really a course imbalance
Mixing a fresh string with a worn one in the same course, causing a tone and volume mismatch
scenario_contexts: Prepping a 12-string guitar before recording so each pair rings evenly
Diagnosing a beating, phasey chord on a mandolin during tracking
Checking octave-pair balance after changing one broken string

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (course)
Baines, The Oxford Companion to Musical Instruments

fields.definition: Unwanted residual sound that remains audible even though a source or channel has been muted, for example a damped or muted note still leaking into other open microphones, or a console/DAW mute that does not fully attenuate the signal.
fields.plain_english: Sound you still hear even after something has been muted. It sneaks through because the mute is not complete, or because it leaks into a nearby mic.
fields.purpose_function: The term names a common capture and mixing fault so engineers can track down why a supposedly silenced part is still audible and fix the routing, gating, or mic setup.
fields.practical_application: When a palm-muted guitar or a muted string still shows up in the drum or room mics, an engineer improves isolation, repositions mics, or gates the offending channel to stop the bleed.
common_mistakes: Assuming a channel mute removes a sound that is actually leaking into other open mics
Relying on a noise gate to hide mute bleed instead of improving isolation at the source
Confusing intentional palm-mute tone with unwanted mute bleed
scenario_contexts: Tracking a full band live, where a muted guitar amp still bleeds into the drum overheads
Editing a multitrack and hearing a muted section still faintly present
Setting up mic screens or isolation to reduce bleed from a damped instrument

fields.definition: Leakage from a device's built-in (onboard) loudspeaker, such as a combo amplifier, keyboard, or practice amp with an integrated speaker, into microphones capturing other sources on a session. It is a specific form of mic bleed caused by the source monitoring itself through its own speaker.
fields.plain_english: When a mic picks up sound coming from a speaker built into an instrument or amp nearby. That built-in speaker leaks into recordings of other things in the room.
fields.purpose_function: The term pinpoints the source of unwanted leakage so an engineer can isolate or reposition the noisy built-in speaker and keep other tracks clean.
fields.practical_application: To stop onboard speaker bleed, a tech turns down or mutes the built-in speaker, uses a DI or line out instead, or moves the device out of the live room.
common_mistakes: UNSAFE: Draping blankets over a tube amp's vents or built-in speaker to block bleed, which traps heat and creates a fire and burn hazard
Forgetting a keyboard's onboard speaker is on and letting it leak into vocal mics
Assuming a DI signal is bleed-free while the instrument's own speaker still feeds the room
scenario_contexts: Recording vocals while a guitarist's combo amp speaker leaks into the vocal mic
Capturing a DI keyboard part while its onboard speaker bleeds into room mics
Isolating an amp in a separate room to remove its speaker bleed from drum mics

fields.definition: The difference in output level between one patch (preset/program) and another on a synthesizer, sampler, or amp/effects modeler, so that switching patches changes the perceived loudness even at the same played dynamics.
fields.plain_english: When you switch sounds on a synth or modeler, some presets are louder than others. That change in volume between presets is patch level variation.
fields.purpose_function: Recognizing this helps players and engineers level-match presets so a performance stays consistent and no patch jumps out or disappears in the mix.
fields.practical_application: Before a session or show, a tech auditions each patch and adjusts its output or a gain stage so all patches sit at a similar level when switched.
common_mistakes: Assuming all factory patches are level-matched out of the box
Setting record levels on one loud patch and then clipping or under-recording quieter ones
Confusing patch level variation with a performer simply playing louder
scenario_contexts: Level-matching amp-modeler presets before tracking a guitar
Balancing synth patches during a live set so no sound jumps out
Gain-staging a keyboard rig where presets differ in output

fields.definition: A small, reusable, self-adhesive gel pad applied to a vibrating surface, most often a drumhead, to absorb vibration and tame unwanted overtones, ring, and sustain. The best-known example is the Moongel-type damping pad.
fields.plain_english: A soft, sticky gel square you press onto a drum to calm down extra ringing. It works like putting a finger on a wine glass to stop it humming.
fields.purpose_function: It gives a quick, removable way to control overtones and shorten sustain without permanently altering the head, so a drum or surface sounds more focused on the recording.
fields.practical_application: An engineer sticks one or more gel dampers near the edge of a snare or tom head, moving or adding pads until the ring is controlled without deadening the tone.
common_mistakes: Using too many gel dampers and deadening the drum completely
Placing the gel in the center of the head instead of near the edge, killing tone and volume
Assuming a gel damper replaces proper drum tuning
scenario_contexts: Taming snare ring during a tracking session
Controlling tom overtones for a tighter recorded sound
Quickly adjusting damping between takes without changing heads

sources: Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (drum damping/muffling)

fields.definition: Elongation of a cymbal's central mounting hole into a keyhole shape, caused by repeated metal-to-metal contact between the cymbal and an unprotected stand rod. The deformation weakens the cymbal and can lead to cracks radiating from the center hole.
fields.plain_english: When a cymbal is mounted on a bare metal rod, the constant banging slowly stretches its center hole into a keyhole shape. That worn hole can weaken the cymbal and make it crack.
fields.purpose_function: Knowing about keyholing tells techs to protect the mounting point with a sleeve and felts, preventing costly cymbal damage and sudden failures during a session.
fields.practical_application: A drum tech checks cymbals for an oval, worn center hole and always mounts them with a plastic or rubber sleeve and felt washers above and below to prevent keyholing.
common_mistakes: Mounting a cymbal directly on a bare metal rod with no plastic sleeve
Tightening the wing nut so hard the cymbal cannot move, which speeds up hole wear and cracking
Ignoring an oval, elongated center hole until the cymbal cracks
scenario_contexts: Inspecting a drummer's cymbals before a session for keyholing damage
Fitting new sleeves and felts to prevent hole wear on a touring kit
Diagnosing a crack that started at a worn, keyholed center hole

sources: Zildjian cymbal care and setup guidance

fields.definition: The designation of a particular song or mix as the A-side, the featured and promoted primary track of a single release, as opposed to the secondary B-side. The term originates from the two sides of a vinyl single, the A-side being the side intended for airplay and promotion.
fields.plain_english: Picking which song is the main track of a single release, the one meant for radio and promotion. It comes from old records, where the A-side was the hit side.
fields.purpose_function: Assigning the A-side sets which track gets priority in mastering, marketing, and delivery, guiding how time and polish are spent.
fields.practical_application: When delivering a single, the team confirms the A-side assignment so the lead track is mastered, labeled, and submitted to platforms as the primary release.
common_mistakes: Thinking the A-side must be the first song recorded rather than the chosen lead track
Assuming only the A-side needs careful mastering, when the B-side should also meet spec
Confusing A-side/B-side (release role) with the A/B of monitor or mix comparison
scenario_contexts: Deciding which single from a session is promoted as the lead A-side
Labeling and delivering master files with the correct A-side and B-side
Planning a vinyl single's sides for a release

sources: Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (disc recording/mastering)

fields.definition: The share of a recorded or monitored sound that arises from real acoustic (airborne) sound, the natural tone of an instrument and its room, as distinct from a direct or electronic signal such as a DI feed. It describes how much of the result comes from air-moving sound versus a captured electrical signal.
fields.plain_english: The part of a sound that comes from real air moving in a room, like a mic on an instrument, rather than a direct plugged-in signal. It is the natural, in-the-room part of the sound.
fields.purpose_function: Separating the acoustic contribution from direct signal lets an engineer blend natural room tone and direct clarity, and control how live or dry a track feels.
fields.practical_application: When recording an electric bass or an acoustic-electric guitar, an engineer blends the DI with a mic to dial in the right amount of acoustic contribution.
common_mistakes: Ignoring the room's acoustic contribution and wondering why a DI-only track sounds lifeless
Blending mic and DI without checking polarity, so the acoustic contribution partly cancels
Assuming a close mic captures no room, when it always adds some acoustic contribution
scenario_contexts: Blending a bass DI with a mic'd cabinet to add acoustic contribution
Deciding how much room mic to fold into a drum mix
Recording an acoustic-electric guitar and balancing pickup with a mic

fields.definition: The use of AI or machine-learning tools to analyze a mix and automatically adjust its loudness to hit a target, usually an integrated loudness in LUFS defined by standards such as ITU-R BS.1770 and EBU R128, often as part of automated mastering or loudness-matching services.
fields.plain_english: Software that uses AI to measure how loud a song is and set it to the right level on its own. It aims for the loudness targets that streaming services expect.
fields.purpose_function: It speeds up loudness matching and normalization so tracks meet platform targets consistently, without an engineer setting every level by hand.
fields.practical_application: An engineer runs a mix through an AI loudness or mastering tool to reach a streaming target, then checks the result against a compliant metering standard.
common_mistakes: Trusting an AI loudness result without checking it on a compliant LUFS meter
Pushing loudness so high the AI tool adds audible distortion or pumping
Assuming one loudness target fits every platform, when specs differ
scenario_contexts: Normalizing a batch of tracks to a streaming LUFS target with an AI tool
Using an AI mastering service to loudness-match songs across an album
Checking an AI-set level against ITU-R BS.1770 metering before delivery

sources: EBU R128; AES streaming loudness recommendations (TD1008)
